- When sentiment is positive (≥0.27) and forecast is rising sharply, reduce peak overshoot by 5–10% to avoid overreacting to short-term sentiment.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.00) and forecast is falling, avoid excessive downward bias — adjust downward by ≤3% to prevent premature sell-off.
- For 30-day forecasts, if recent 18-day history shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 2–3 consecutive days of price decline), model should not overcorrect upward — cap forecast rise to 1–2% above recent mean.
- When sentiment is volatile (alternating +/–0.27), avoid averaging or smoothing — instead, weight recent 5-day sentiment more heavily to capture momentum.
- If forecast spikes >10% above recent 18-day average, flag for correction — especially if sentiment is neutral or negative — to prevent overconfidence in momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from forecast in first 5 days, adjust subsequent days downward if sentiment remains weak or neutral — avoid “early overcorrection” bias.
- If sentiment is consistently positive over 3+ days, allow forecast to rise but cap at 15% above 18-day average — prevent “sentiment-driven inflation” in price.
- If forecast is consistently below true outcome (e.g., 3+ days), check sentiment — if sentiment is weak or negative, consider increasing forecast by 2–3% to align with sentiment shift.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome shows strong upward trend (e.g., >5% rise in 5 days), model should not lag — adjust forecast to match sentiment momentum, even if historical mean suggests otherwise.
